title: Concurrency in Java: code drills
seriesDescription: Threads, synchronized, locks, volatile, executors, CompletableFuture, virtual threads, concurrent collections and classic drills. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Write-the-code drills: producer-consumer with BlockingQueue and wait/notify, Conditions, a thread-safe LRU cache, a token-bucket rate limiter, odd/even printing and print-in-order.
source: Oracle Java docs (BlockingQueue, LinkedHashMap, Condition, CountDownLatch); Java Concurrency in Practice; Baeldung; GeeksforGeeks; LeetCode concurrency problems (print in order, odd/even printing)

questions.prompt: A producer thread calls `put()` for the numbers 1..10 on an `ArrayBlockingQueue` with capacity 3. No consumer is running. How many `put()` calls complete before the producer blocks?
questions.explanation: `put()` blocks when the queue is full, so exactly capacity (3) calls return and the fourth waits for a `take()`. That blocking is the back-pressure that makes bounded queues safe.

questions.prompt: Using a `BlockingQueue<Integer>` named `q` (already created, capacity 10), write a producer loop that puts 1..100 and then one -1 sentinel, and a consumer loop that takes items until it sees -1.
questions.explanation: `put/take` block, so no manual locking or sleeping is needed. Both throw `InterruptedException`. `offer/poll` with timeouts are valid but need retry logic.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class `Buffer` holding a `Queue<Integer> q` (a `LinkedList`) and a `final int cap`, with `synchronized` `put(int x)` and `take()` methods using `wait()` and `notifyAll()`. `put` must wait while the queue is full, `take` while it is empty. Both methods throw `InterruptedException`.

checks.label: waits in a while loop, not an if
handles both the full and the empty condition

questions.explanation: Verified to run correctly with a producer and consumer thread. `notifyAll` is safer than `notify` because producers and consumers share one wait set. Using `ReentrantLock` with two `Conditions` (`notFull`, `notEmpty`) is the cleaner alternative.

questions.prompt: In the wait/notify buffer, why must the guard be `while (q.isEmpty()) wait();` rather than `if (q.isEmpty()) wait();`?

options.text: A woken thread must re-test the condition, as another consumer may have taken the item or the wake-up was spurious.
options.why: Correct: the condition can be false again by the time the woken thread reacquires the monitor.

options.text: The Java compiler rejects a call to `wait()` that is not placed inside a loop body, so an if statement would not even compile.
options.why: Nothing in the language requires a loop around `wait()`.

options.text: The loop makes the monitor fair, so waiting threads wake in arrival order.
options.why: Looping has no influence on fairness; it only re-tests the predicate.

options.text: `notify()` will not wake any thread unless the guard around `wait()` is a loop.
options.why: `notify()` wakes a waiter regardless of how the guard is written.

questions.explanation: Always wait in a loop on the predicate. The same rule applies to `Condition.await()` with a `ReentrantLock`.

questions.prompt: One producer feeds a shared queue that 4 consumer threads read, and consumers stop when they take a poison pill. How many pills must the producer enqueue after the last real item so that every consumer terminates?
questions.explanation: A consumer that takes a pill exits and never takes another, so each consumer needs its own pill: 4. (Re-queueing one pill is the alternative.)

questions.text: Create a LinkedHashMap with accessOrder set to {1}, override {2} to return size() > capacity, and make it thread-safe by synchronizing every method or wrapping it with Collections.{3}.
questions.explanation: With access order, `get()` moves the entry to the tail, so the head is the least recently used. `removeEldestEntry` is the hook called after each put. `ConcurrentHashMap` alone cannot give you LRU ordering.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: In a `LinkedHashMap` with `accessOrder=true`, even `get()` needs the same lock as `put()`.
questions.reason: In access-order mode `get()` relinks the entry to the end of the list, which is a structural modification.

whys.a: Correct: get() mutates the linked list, so reads cannot run in parallel; a ReadWriteLock read lock would be wrong.
whys.b: R is the direct cause of A, so b understates the relationship.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: This is why a `ReadWriteLock` does not help an LRU cache: every hit is a write to recency order.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class `LruCache<K,V>` with a constructor `LruCache(int cap)`, `synchronized V get(K k)` and `synchronized void put(K k, V v)`. Back it with a `LinkedHashMap` in access order that evicts the eldest entry when size exceeds cap.

checks.label: overrides removeEldestEntry with a size check
get and put are synchronized (or locked)

questions.explanation: Verified: after `put a, put b, get a, put c` with capacity 2 the cache holds `{a, c}`. Subclassing `LinkedHashMap` and wrapping in `Collections.synchronizedMap` is another accepted design.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class `OddEven` with a field `int next = 1`, a `final int max`, and one `synchronized` method `print(boolean odd) throws InterruptedException` that two threads call (one with `true`, one with `false`) so numbers 1..max are printed alternately using `wait()` and `notifyAll()`.
questions.explanation: Verified for `max = 9`. The final `notifyAll` lets the other thread see `next > max` and exit. Two `Semaphores` are a simpler valid answer.

questions.prompt: Write a thread-safe Java class `TokenBucket(double cap, double rate)` whose tokens start full and refill at `rate` tokens per second up to `cap`. `boolean allow()` refills lazily from the elapsed `System.nanoTime()`, consumes one token if at least one is available and returns `true`, otherwise `false`.
questions.explanation: Verified: a bucket of 3 answers true, true, true, false, false for five instant calls. Refill and consume are one read-modify-write, so they share the lock. An `AtomicLong` holding the next-allowed time with a `CAS` loop is the lock-free variant.

questions.prompt: Three threads run `first()`, `second()` and `third()` in an arbitrary start order, but the output must always be first, second, third. Given `CountDownLatch l1` and `l2` (each `new CountDownLatch(1)`), write the three methods; each prints its own name and may throw `InterruptedException`.
questions.explanation: Each latch is a one-shot gate that later steps wait on. Verified with threads started in the order third, first, second. `Semaphores` with zero permits, or a monitor with a turn variable, also work.
questions.starter: CountDownLatch l1 = new CountDownLatch(1), l2 = new CountDownLatch(1);

questions.prompt: An access-ordered LRU cache with capacity 2 receives `put(1)`, `put(2)`, `get(1)`, `put(3)`, `put(4)`. What is the sum of the keys still cached?
questions.explanation: After `get(1)` the order is 2, 1; `put(3)` evicts 2; `put(4)` evicts 1 (the least recently used), leaving 3 and 4, so the sum is 7 (verified with a `LinkedHashMap`).

questions.prompt: A bounded buffer uses one `ReentrantLock` with two `Conditions`, `notFull` and `notEmpty`, instead of `wait()` and `notifyAll()` on the buffer. What is the main benefit?

options.text: `Condition.await()` can be called without holding the lock, which saves a lock acquisition.
options.why: `await()` requires the lock and releases it `while` waiting, like `wait()` does.

options.text: Using two `Conditions` makes the lock fair, so waiting threads proceed in arrival order.
options.why: Fairness is chosen with `new ReentrantLock(true)`, not by the number of `Conditions`.

options.text: Each Condition gets its own separate lock, so producers and consumers can never block each other at all.
options.why: Both `Conditions` belong to the same lock; they only split the `wait` sets.

options.text: Waiters are split into two groups, so `signal()` wakes only a thread that can proceed.
options.why: Correct: a consumer signalling `notFull` never wakes other consumers, avoiding wasted wake-ups and the need for `notifyAll`.

questions.explanation: Always await in a `while` loop on the predicate. A bounded buffer built this way is the textbook alternative to `ArrayBlockingQueue`.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A bounded `BlockingQueue` gives producers back-pressure when consumers fall behind.
questions.reason: A `LinkedBlockingQueue` stores its elements in linked nodes rather than in an array.

whys.a: R is a true storage fact, but it does not explain why a full queue slows producers.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is unrelated to A; put() blocks (or offer fails) because the queue is full.
whys.c: R is true, so option c (R false) is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so option d (A false) is wrong.

questions.explanation: Back-pressure comes from the capacity bound: `put()` blocks, `offer()` returns false, `add()` throws. An unbounded queue turns overload into memory growth instead.
